set.longDescription:
Between 1793 and 1906 European and American missionary societies planted churches across India, West Africa, the Pacific and the China coast. And almost immediately those churches began to be run, staffed and spread by local Christians the societies had not planned for. Samuel Ajayi Crowther, enslaved as a boy in Yorubaland and freed by an anti-slavery patrol, translated the Bible into Yoruba and in 1864 became the first African Anglican bishop, only for the next generation of the same society to force him aside in 1890. In the Pacific it was hundreds of Polynesian teachers, not Europeans, who carried Christianity from island to island, often at the cost of their lives. In China the preacher Liang Fa wrote a tract in 1832 whose stray reading by Hong Xiuquan helped set the Taiping upheaval in motion, and the former opium addict known as Pastor Xi built a network of his own converts inland. What holds these four wings together is a single problem. Nearly everything written about them was written from the mission's side, and the native voices that do survive are what any honest telling has to be built on.

Liberia's settler church belongs to the West African wing. It came from America. Lott Cary was born a slave near Richmond, Virginia, about 1780, and the church there encouraged him to preach. About 1815 he helped rouse the Black Christians of Richmond to take an interest in Africa. The Richmond African Missionary Society that followed gave between one hundred and one hundred and fifty dollars to the African mission for several years. In 1821 Cary sailed for West Africa. In a letter from Free Town he wrote, 'Before we left the United States, we formed ourselves into a church'. On 16 August 1823 he wrote from Monrovia, 'Our little church has been wonderfully blessed of late.' He had baptized two the day before. Cary's words reach us through a biography by J. B. Taylor, a Richmond Baptist pastor, printed in 1837.

Korea lies outside the four wings, but its Protestant church began in these same years. Before the first missionaries came, two Scots at Mukden, Ross and McIntyre, had done introductory work in China among Koreans. Some Koreans there took up the faith. They began work in Korean villages on the China side of the Yalu. Ross and McIntyre translated a number of the Gospels, and later the whole New Testament.

Underwood, who reached Korea in 1885, says in his book of 1908 that Dr. Allen settled in Seoul in September 1884. He adds that the Methodists sent Dr. McClay from Japan to look over the field in that same year.

The first converts, in July and the fall of 1886, were baptized behind closed doors. The old law of death to Christians had never been repealed. It seemed plain that it would not be enforced, but no one knew how far to venture.

A Korean colporteur, Soh Sang Ryun, told Underwood of 'a small company of Christians' at Sorai. By 1890 the two churches had over one hundred converts in all Korea. In 1896 the missionaries' monthly in Seoul spoke of inquirers who had 'finished the study of the Ross catechism'. It was The Korean Repository. All of this comes to us in the missionaries' own telling.

set.longDescription:
The Church of England entered the nineteenth century as a comfortable establishment and left it a contested one. Three parties argued for its soul. Evangelicals who had inherited the awakening's fervor and its campaigns against slavery and squalor, high churchmen who rediscovered the church's catholic inheritance, and broad churchmen who wanted room for the new biblical criticism and the new geology. The quarrels went to law: the Gorham case of 1850 over what baptism does, the storm over the essayists of 1860 who applied critical methods to Scripture, ritual prosecutions that put clergymen in prison over vestments and candles. Underneath the controversies the church rebuilt itself, in thousands of new buildings and slum parishes at home and in a mission network abroad that by 1867 had produced enough overseas bishops that a first Lambeth Conference had to be called to hold them together.

Samuel Marsden shows the church reaching overseas. A pamphlet of his, printed in 1826 by his biographer's account, calls him 'principal Chaplain to the Colony of New South Wales'. His biographer dates one letter to 7 October 1814, just before Marsden sailed for New Zealand. In it Marsden wrote that he had 'submitted my views to the Church Missionary Society, and solicited their aid.'

On Christmas Day, in 1814 by the biographer's date, Marsden preached in New Zealand. He wrote, 'In this manner, the Gospel has been introduced into New Zealand'. On 5 June 1815 he wrote from Parramatta that the societies in London could not make up their minds to send out a vessel. So he 'at last determined to purchase one for the purpose on my own account'.

In April 1837 he asked a missionary, 'Have they any meeting in the week-days for prayer and religious instruction?' The quoted words are Marsden's own, printed in a biography of 1913. Three of the dates are the biographer's. The book tells the mission from one side only. The Maori side is not in it.

CATHOLIC AFTER 1886 (report for the coordinator; no Catholic line is drafted and VIII.21's dates are unchanged). What the Library's Korean sources say:

Korean Repository 1896, file lines 11636: the treaty ('Franco-Korean treaty') 'opened a new era to the Catholic religion': 'The conclusion of the Franco-Korean treaty, in giving to the French missionaries the right of holding property, of building and residing in the Capital and in the open ports, and of travelling freoly and openly thro the whole country, opened a new era to the Catholic religion.' (OCR 'freoly' kept.) This is in the obituary of Father Coste, a Paris Foreign Missions priest, translated from the French by Mrs. Alexander Kenmure (title block at file lines 11149-11165), so it is a Catholic voice printed in the Protestants' monthly. The treaty's year is NOT given in the passage; the passage does not say 1886.

Korean Repository 1896, Coste obituary, building after the treaty: file lines 11662: 'in 1888, a temporary chapel was built and opened for services'; file lines 11668: 'rose from the ground in 1891'; file lines 11677-11678: 'in the spring of 1892, had the joy of beinp^ able to lay and to bless at Seoul the first stone of the Cathedral' (OCR garbles 'beinp^' and the bishop's name; 'In 1887, a hill was almost razed' is in the same passage). Coste died 28 February 1896 (header at file line 11165, 'Died Febniar>' garbled). The OCR of this passage is damaged in many lines; only these short strings are clean enough to quote.

Korean Repository 1896, Catholic schools and seminary of Paris Foreign Missions in Seoul: file lines 22590: 'a Latin school bad been opened in 1885'; file lines 22552-22553: 'The object of the school is to train into good Catholics these unfortunate children'. The article is 'Education in the Capital of Korea' (file line 22472, 'EDUCATION IN THE CAPITAL OF KOEEA'); most of its Catholic paragraph is too garbled to quote (file lines 22540-22650).

Korean Repository 1896, a Protestant view of the toleration: file lines 31386: 'Toleration in religious matters has marked the reign of' (the article on the King of Korea; its next lines say Catholic Christians were slaughtered under the Tai Won Kan but are OCR-garbled and not quotable).

Underwood 1908, Catholic numbers and the toleration: file lines 4686-4687: 'At first secretly, but since the opening of Korea by treaty more publicly'; file lines 4688-4689: 'in 1901, the reported number of Roman Catholic Christians was over 42,000' (the only post-1886 Catholic fact in the book; he adds that the count includes all baptized infants, file line 4694). file lines 4919-4920: 'A reaction had set in since the persecutions of 1866'; file lines 4922-4923: 'The old law of death to the Christian had never been repealed' (said of the whole country in 1884-86 and about Protestants, but it is the only 'toleration' passage). file lines 4676-4677: 'a Roman Catholic Church has since been erected' (on the hill by the little west gate where the martyrs died; undated).

WHAT THIS ADDS UP TO: the Library holds one clean dated Catholic count (over 42,000 in 1901, Underwood) and a Catholic obituary that gives building dates (temporary chapel 1888, seminary 1891, cathedral foundation stone spring 1892) and the treaty as the start of open mission. It does not give the year of the treaty or toleration in these passages, and Underwood does not treat the Catholic church after 1886 beyond the 1901 count. A Catholic line could carry: the treaty's effect (quoted), the building dates, and the 1901 count. Whether to enter that at the end of VIII.21's story (which would run past its window of 1784-1886) or hold is the coordinator's decision; VIII.21's status text says the 1886-1904 gap is 'disclosed for a later entry, not absorbed here'.

DALLET AND VIII.21 (shelf use only, nothing drafted): Dallet (1874, French, to 1866) supports VIII.21's existing text in part. Yi Sung-hun's baptism in Beijing and his return in 1784: file lines 15463: 'Au printemps de l'année kap-tsin (1784), Pierre Seng-houn-i'; his baptism of the others: file lines 15624-15625: 'qui avait reçu le baptême à Péking, conféra lui-même ce sacrement k Piek-i' (OCR 'k' for 'à' kept); no priest had ever preached there: file lines 16112: 'd'un royaume où jamais aucun prêtre n'avait'; 'more than four thousand' Christians ten years after the Beijing baptism: file lines 17715-17716: 'plus de quatre mille chrétiens en Corée' (VIII.21 says 'several thousand'). Not checked in the pages read: the Confucian scholars as the first circle, Chong Yak-chong's vernacular catechism, the 'ten thousand killed' figure, and the 1886 treaty (Dallet ends at 1866). Dallet's name for the first convert is 'Seng-houn-i' (Pierre Ni), not 'Yi Sung-hun', and Underwood says the first Korean baptized in Beijing in 1783 was named Peter (file line 4612: 'the first Korean was baptized and named Peter'), one year earlier than VIII.21's 1784.
